newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: U.N blames Guatemalan army for last rebel death.
newsitem.headline: U.N blames Guatemalan army for last rebel death.

text.p: Elite army officials illegally captured and probably killed a rebel commander during the final round of peace talks in Guatemala late last year, the U.N. human rights mission here said on Tuesday.

The United Nations Mission for Verification of Human Rights in Guatemala (Minugua) leveled the charges after a three-week probe into the case of a missing guerrilla, whose fate has become a national obsession.

Juan Jose Cabrera Rodas, known as Commander Mincho, was probably the final casualty of the 36-year armed rebellion that ended with the signing of an historic peace agreement on Dec. 29, a report said.

"This mission's verification, the methods used in similar operations, and the significance of the case lead to the conclusion that (Cabrera and another rebel) were captured by security forces," the Minugua report said.
While newspapers speculated about Cabrera's rumoured torture and assassination in the hands of state security forces, the government and former rebels denied he existed.
Mincho and his comrade-in-arms, Augusto Rafael Baldizon, were seized by government security forces on Oct. 19, the report said.

The men were most likely captured for their alleged involvement in a kidnapping which took place during a tense ceasefire between government and rebels and almost derailed the peace process in its final stretch.
The government broke off talks for two weeks until the rebels apologised for the abduction of Olga de Novella, an 86-year-old matriarch of an influential Guatemalan family.
Baldizon was freed in exchange for de Novella, but Cabrera never reappeared. He was likely killed during capture, the U.N. report said.
"The mission has received various versions of events that coincide in indicating that Mr. Cabrera died at the time of his capture," the report added.

The Presidential Guard, which acts independently of the army, has denied being involved in Cabrera's disappearance. The report said the group continued to act as an illegal, clandestine security force.
The case has been an embarrassment to the government and leaders of the Guatemala National Revolutionary Unit (URNG), the former leftist rebels' group seeking to become a political party.
